prize_parts.citation: for foundational contributions to the analysis of nominal rigidities and monetary policy: time-dependent price setting, staggered contracts and policy rules, and a micro-founded theory of optimal monetary policy

statement.case_for: I have changed my preferred configuration from B003 (Kiyotaki, Moore) to B014 (Calvo, Taylor, Woodford). The change rests on two points in my own round-1 reasoning, not on the number of colleagues now preferring B014. First, my main objection to B014 was attribution: with six or seven strong claimants, a three-person cap looked arbitrary. The exchange showed that the objection can be handled by drafting. Calvo's pricing friction, Taylor's contracts and policy rule, and Woodford's micro-founded normative synthesis are three separately identifiable, load-bearing components, and a citation can name them as components without claiming the estimated-DSGE tradition. I wrote in round 1 that I would prefer B014 if a defensible three-person attribution could be agreed. I now judge the component-based attribution defensible, though not costless. Second, on the common criteria of originality, durability and breadth of tested influence, B014 has the larger footprint. It has been used and revised through 2008, the zero lower bound and the post-2021 inflation, and it is the baseline that later critiques are built against. B003 remains a clean, original and mature mechanism, and I still think it is distinct from the 2022 prize. But a distinct mechanism does not by itself establish priority over a larger, repeatedly tested body of work. I treat the six explicit B014 preferences in the chair summary only as a signal that the attribution question was tractable for colleagues across specialities. They are not evidence of merit. I am a political scientist and rely on colleagues' accounts of the macro literature for priority. I have tried to rest the change on arguments I could assess, namely whether the three roles are distinct and whether the citation can be worded to match them.
statement.case_against: The cost of exclusion is real and not resolved by wording. Galí, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Evans, Smets, Wouters and Gertler made major contributions. Andersson is right that the Christiano-Eichenbaum-Evans work on identifying monetary shocks and estimating a medium-scale model is a different kind of contribution from the three components named, and a component-based citation implicitly places it outside the award. Calvo versus Galí as the third name remains a defensible judgement call. Identification in estimated DSGE models rests on strong structural assumptions, so the framework's empirical record is mixed, and I do not want to overstate how 'tested' it is. Representative-agent versions may be seen as superseded by heterogeneous-agent work, so a prize could reward a stage in the field's development. The 2022 prize and earlier macro prizes may also narrow marginal room, although I find the argument that none of them recognised the pricing friction and policy rule persuasive. B003, by contrast, has an undisputed two-person attribution and a single identifiable origin. If the committee cannot agree on a narrow citation for B014, B003 is the cleaner prize and I would support it.

responses.point: Krusell argues that Calvo (pricing device), Taylor (contracts and rule) and Woodford (microfounded synthesis and welfare-based policy) are three distinct conceptual steps. He treats Galí as the strongest omitted claimant and says saturation by earlier macro prizes is a smaller concern than attribution.
responses.response: The 'three distinct steps' argument is what moved me. It turns my round-1 worry, that any trio is arbitrary, into a question of what the citation says it credits. I accept it on that basis. I do not accept that it removes the cost of excluding Galí, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets, and you concede that cost yourself. I also note that your own field, heterogeneous-agent macro, extends or criticises this framework, as your disclosure says. I have therefore tried to rely on the structure of the argument and not on the fact that you hold it. On saturation, I agree your list of earlier awards (expectations, time consistency, identification, banking crises) leaves the pricing friction and the rule unrecognised.

responses.point: Andersson moved from Woodford, Taylor and Galí to Calvo, Taylor and Woodford. He argues that Christiano-Eichenbaum-Evans is not derivative, because it concerns identifying monetary shocks and estimating a medium-scale model. He treats this as a real cost of the three-person cap, not a resolved question.
responses.response: I take that qualification as the most important caveat on my new position. Whether the citation implicitly ranks the estimated-model tradition below the three named components is unresolved, and I do not want to claim otherwise. My answer to the chair's wording question is that the citation should say what it rewards, namely the pricing friction, contract and rule analysis, and the micro-founded theory of policy, and should not say 'the New Keynesian framework' as a whole. This reduces the implied ranking but does not eliminate it. If you or others think the cap makes the problem unresolvable, I would want to hear the specific wording that fails.

responses.point: Strömberg prefers the Kiyotaki-Moore pair, like me. He concedes that B014 has the largest footprint in institutional practice and says he would support B014 if the committee found a defensible narrower citation. He also argues that the 2022 prize is about banks as intermediaries, whereas Kiyotaki-Moore is about borrowers' collateral.
responses.response: We stated the same condition in round 1, and I think the component-based wording above meets it, though you will need to judge that yourself. I still agree with you that B003 is a different discovery from the 2022 prize. My move does not rest on the claim that the 2022 prize sinks B003. It rests on B014's attribution turning out to be more tractable than I thought, and on its larger tested footprint. Your point on the limited direct empirical identification of the original Kiyotaki-Moore paper is one I raised myself, and it bears on maturity weighting even though I do not treat it as disqualifying. B003 remains my first alternative.

responses.point: Hassler distinguishes the earlier awards (Lucas, Sargent and Sims on expectations and identification, Kydland and Prescott on time consistency, Bernanke 2022 on banks and crises). He argues none recognised the pricing friction and policy-rule framework. He asks why collateral-constraint dynamics should take priority over recognising the monetary policy framework.
responses.response: That question was fair, and my round-1 answer was incomplete. I had argued that the collateral-constraint mechanism is distinct from the 2022 work, and I still believe that. Distinctness is necessary but not sufficient for priority. Once I accept your point that the pricing-friction and rule core is also unrecognised, the comparison turns on breadth of tested influence and attribution tractability, and there B014 now looks stronger to me. I note that you co-author with the secretary and with Boppart and Friberg, and that your chair role means your preference is one among six, as the chair summary says. I have tried not to treat your position as evidence of merit.

responses.point: Fredriksson, replying to my round-1 position, accepts the narrower Kiyotaki-Moore pair but disagrees that the 2022 overlap is serious. He argues that collateral-driven amplification differs from bank runs and from the Depression-era credit-channel work.
responses.response: I largely agree with you, and it is why I list B003 first among my alternatives and not lower. I would not want B003 dismissed on overlap grounds, because the committee would be applying a prior-prize standard that, as the chair's question asks, should be applied consistently across the 2008 trade prize, the 2022 prize, the 2024 prize and the game-theory prizes. My change of preference comes from the comparative judgement on attribution and tested footprint, and not from regarding B003 as already honoured.

uncertainties: Whether Calvo or Galí is the better third name, and whether a citation weighted toward the empirical and estimated framework would change the trio. I cannot settle this from the supplied evidence, and Hjalmarsson and Hassler have said they would be open to a swap.

Whether any three-person citation can avoid implicitly ranking Christiano, Eichenbaum, Evans, Smets, Wouters and Gertler below the named laureates. My component-based wording reduces but does not remove this.

How to read the post-2021 inflation and the heterogeneous-agent critique: as extensions of the credited contributions, which is my current reading, or as grounds for caution on maturity. I lack the technical standing to decide this on my own and rely on colleagues' accounts.
Whether the 2022 prize leaves room for B003, which affects how strong an alternative it is, and whether the committee applies a consistent prior-prize standard across entries.
My attribution and priority judgements on the macro literature come from colleagues' round-1 statements and my own background reading. I have not independently verified them against primary sources.
statement.conflict_note: No connection to Calvo, Taylor or Woodford is apparent from my supplied profile. B003 and B014 are outside my field, which is political science, so I rely on common criteria and colleagues' expositions. For the alternative B032, my profile lists a co-authored Governance paper on corruption as a collective-action problem with Torsten Persson and Bo Rothstein. Persson is at Stockholm University, in a different department from mine, and B032 is close to my own field of comparative political institutions. I disclose this and do not adjudicate it. It is why B032 is an alternative and not my preferred configuration. I also gave the 2024 presentation speech, which may reflect collective drafting and does not indicate a prize preference. I have no apparent link to the B003 laureates, and my move from B003 to B014 does not rest on any connection.
